# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-26 (Extended v182)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to summer Year 7. Primary locations include Paris—Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue du Pont-aux-Choux, Rue de Thorigny, Marché Saint-Jean, Rue des Billettes, Rue Saint-Denis, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Rue de la Petite-Truanderie, Rue Mondétour, Pointe Saint-Eustache, Rue du Cygne, Rue des Prêcheurs, Rue Blomet, Rue de Rivoli, Place Louis XV, Champs-Élysées, Esplanade, bridge of the Invalides, Hôtel des Princes, Hôtel Meurice, Rue Saint-Honoré, Passage Delorme, Place du Palais-Royal, Rue de Béthisy, Rue des Bourdonnais, Rue de la Poterie, Rue du Contrat-Social, Marché-aux-Poirées, Rue de Babylone, Rue du Chaume, Rue des Vieilles-Haudriettes, Royal Printing Establishment. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Wilholt, Torton, Quenford, Pontoise, Stenenridge, Gulhaven.

**Rumored claims (unverified)**: Yera Stenworth confided fire at Dunstead granary set deliberately (winter Year 5). Fenelle Lindmere and Marald confided/revealed Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family. **Late one night Ferald Stenworth confided to Zavus Prydenridge that the Stenson family once owed a blood debt to the Stenenridge family**. Stenenridge mill ledger rewritten after flood (autumn Year 6).

**Established facts**: Kassa Brackick and Volan Stenworth married at Staveford; Kassa later went to Dungate. Taric Corrley quit Staveford, took lodgings in Dungate. Marald Corrford quit Dunstead, took lodgings in Salcombe; Fenelle Lindmere followed within month. Ismira Stenson quit Dungate, took lodgings in Elmhaven (winter Year 6). Matho Stenson went to Elmhaven (winter Year 6). Elra Corrford settled in Elmhaven. Havie Prydenridge promised Gadrek Prydenridge to pay old debt to Stenworth family. Thizek Stenenridge told Elra Corrford deed to Kelmere pastures was forged. Kassa Stenson's husband gave solemn promise to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe. Fenelle Lindmere found work in Elmhaven, moved there, did not return to Salcombe (summer Year 7). Marald Corrford followed to Elmhaven within the month (summer Year 7).

**Solemn promises (established)**: Elra Corrford gave Matho Stenson solemn promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven. Pelia gave Fenelle solemn promise to plant orchard on slope above Salcombe (summer Year 7).

**New births and marriages (Spring Year 7)**: Rinelle Corrley and Kadrek Brackick had son Movus Brackick (Wilholt). Nerine Prydenridge and Lurald Stenworth wed at Ostcombe with half parish present, lived in Ostcombe thereafter, had son Istho Stenworth (Ostcombe). Wenelle Lindmere and Rovus Prydenridge had son Febin Prydenridge (Kelmere). Bremira Corrford and Zavus Prydenridge married at Dunstead (before summer Year 7), lived in Dunstead thereafter.

**Spring and Summer Year 7 observations**: Residents walked long way to avoid muddy square. Road rutted and puddled after thaw. Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall (repeated observations). Multiple residents hummed childhood tunes while scrubbing steps (Yera, Rinelle, Zavus, Kadan, Bremira, Rorald Lindmere). Matho, Bremira, Thizek, and Pelia each counted coins twice, came up penny short. **Thizek counted the coins twice and still came up a penny short**. Taric remarked river was up at Dungate crossing; Kassa said it always was in spring. Sebin remarked river was up; Rorald Lindmere said it always was in spring. Ismira and Bremira each argued with carter over price of sack of oats. **Ferald Stenworth argued with the carter over the price of a sack of oats**. Kadan and Rovus talked of weather, harvest, lame horse. Rovus and Kadan discussed scandal of salt prices. Bremira and Ferald discussed scandal of salt prices. **"The price of salt is a scandal," said Yewyn. "A scandal," agreed Pelia**. Yera laughed at story nobody else found funny. Sebin and Rorald Lindmere both laughed at stories nobody else found funny. **Pelia Lindmere laughed at a story nobody else found funny**. Yera Stenworth and Zavus complained of aching backs. Pelia complained of aching back, as usual. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps. Children chased hoop down lane, shrieking. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Yewyn Haskick bought ribbon at stall and regretted it. Tatho Brackick bought ribbon at stall and regretted it. Yewyn appeared tired; Pelia noted this. **Tatho mended torn sleeve by window and said little**. **"Will it rain, do you think?" asked Tatho. Rorald only shrugged**. **Tatho spent the evening sorting old letters by candlelight**. **The baker's boy was late again, and the line at the oven grew long**. **"You look tired," Thizek Stenenridge told Zavus Prydenridge, who did not deny it**. Rorald Lindmere walked long way round to avoid muddy square. **Zavus read the almanac aloud, mispronouncing half the saints**. **Isvie Stenworth fell asleep in the chair before the fire had caught**.

**Summer Year 7 broken faith**: Rorald Lindmere broke faith with Kassa Stenson—promised work (carry sealed letter to Torton) never begun.

## Jean Valjean's Crisis and Discovery
**Blotting-book discovery (night 24th June 1832)**: Upon arriving at Rue de l'Homme Armé lodgings, Valjean found Cosette's blotting-book open on sideboard. Mirror reflection revealed four lines—letter Cosette wrote to young workman in Rue Plumet. Valjean understood Cosette was escaping; another was goal of her heart. Soul gave utter roar. Into paternity his life's widowhood introduced all shades of love—daughter, mother, sister, woman, wife. Grief surpassed bounds; quiver of revolt ran head to foot; immense reawakening of egotism; the *I* howled.

**During Spring Year 7**: Groped up stairs, hand trembling greatly. Unfolded Marius's note announcing death and love. Seized essential points. Beheld splendor of death of hated individual, remained crushed with intoxicated amazement. **Rue de l'Homme Armé lodgings**: Two sleeping-rooms, dining-room, kitchen, garret for Toussaint on second floor, back court. Initially slept well; awoke almost gay; recovered serenity and security. Twice or thrice Toussaint stammered about fighting in Paris—Valjean paid no heed, absorbed in calculations.

**Current state (summer Year 7)**: Valjean asleep; Toussaint has not risen. Cosette's father thought unkind by her. **Valjean at barricade (6th June, dawn)**: Took aim at fireman acting as sentinel on neighboring roof, smashed his helmet with bullet. When officer replaced sentinel, Valjean took aim again, sent officer's casque to join soldier's. Officer retired speedily. No further attempts to spy on barricade made thereafter.

## Marius and Cosette's Romance
**Recognition and love**: Cosette acknowledged she never forgot Marius, always loved him. Beginning autumn Year 5, Marius came every evening, forcing old gate. At height of love's voluptuousness, remained absolutely chaste. **Confessions (spring Year 6, during cholera)**: Marius told Cosette—orphan, name Marius Pontmercy, lawyer, father colonel and hero on bad terms with rich grandfather, hinted at being baron. Cosette told Marius—brought up at Petit-Picpus convent, mother dead, father M. Fauchelevent. **Éponine's death (evening 24th June)**: Éponine revealed she led Marius to barricade, spoke of her death as blessing, protected him from gunfire. Gave Marius letter from Cosette before dying. **Cosette's letter content**: Marriage impossible; grandfather refuses; no fortune either; hastened to him, he gone; kept promise given; dies; loves him. **Marius's response**: Covered letter with kisses; reflected Cosette going to England. Resolved to inform Cosette of death, send farewell, save Gavroche.

**Marius joins barricade (evening 24th June)**: Upon learning Valjean plans England departure in one week, arranged meeting 26th June at nine o'clock. Same evening, displaced bar at grating, rushed in. Cosette absent. Seated self with resolution, blessed love. Mad with grief, one desire: speedy end. Voice summoned him to barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie. **During first phase**: Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed; flung self into conflict. Saved Gavroche with first shot, delivered Courfeyrac with second. Seized powder barrel, dropped flame with startling cry. **Mental state (6th June, dawn)**: Fasting, fevered, emerged from all hope, stranded in grief, saturated with violent emotions, conscious end was near, plunged into visionary stupor voluntarily accepted. Despair's ecstasy. Felt he had entered tomb.

**Cosette's current state (summer Year 7, morning)**: Slept only few hours but soundly; had sweet dreams. Awoke with sun in eyes. First thought smiling. Felt thoroughly reassured. Began cherishing hope without knowing why. Then felt pang at heart. Three days since saw Marius. Certain he would come today, perhaps this very morning. Felt she could not live without Marius. Opened window, looked around hoping to see street. Back court surrounded by high walls, outlook only on gardens. Pronounced gardens hideous; for first time found flowers ugly. Decided to gaze at sky, thought Marius might come from that quarter. Burst into tears. Heard sharp shocks in distance—actually cannon reports battering barricade. **Cosette at window (6th June, dawn)**: Observed martin's nest in ancient cornice below her window. Mother spread wings like fan over brood; father fluttered about, bearing food and kisses. Gilded by dawning day. Great law "Multiply" lay there smiling and august. Sweet mystery unfolded in morning's glory. Cosette, hair in sunlight, soul absorbed in chimæras, illuminated by love within and dawn without, bent over mechanically and began gazing at birds, family, male and female, mother and little ones, with profound trouble virgin nest produces.

## Barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie (24th June into 6th June)
**Café Corinthe**: Ground floor with bar; first floor with billiard-table and spiral staircase; cellar via trap-door; lodgings and attics. Proprietor: Widow Hucheloup. Serving-maids: Matelote, Gibelotte. **Two barricades**: Larger shut off Rue de la Chanvrerie; other closed Rue Mondétour. **Larger barricade (6th June, dawn)**: Height six or seven feet, stepped construction, paling-stones, casks, wheels, omnibus pole with ropes, red flag. Forty-three insurgents. **Three-front fortification**: Walled on Rue de la Chanvrerie (front), Rues du Cygne and de la Petite Truanderie (left), Rue Mondétour (right). Almost impregnable but fatally hemmed in. No exit.

**Javert's arrest**: Identified as Inspector of Police, aged fifty-two. Bound with whip-cord about feet, martingale rope from neck. Upon seeing Valjean surveying him, remarked: "It is perfectly simple."

**Le Cabuc execution**: Enjolras executed him for killing, justified by insurrection needing discipline.

**M. Mabeuf's sacrifice**: Venerable, austere, aged eighty. Evening 24th June: followed band, refused arms. During attack: tore flag from Enjolras, upholding red banner with aged arm. Enjolras eulogized: magnificent death; presence renders barricade impregnable. Body lay in kitchen on table.

**Tactical situation (6th June)**: Unknown messenger announced whole army of Paris striking, third bearing down, National Guard advancing, attack in one hour. After first assault and repairs: insurgents rallied, majority ascended to first-story window. Medical students cared for wounded. Five gravely wounded men on mattresses in kitchen converted to ambulance. Barricade repaired and augmented, raised two feet. No repast possible; fifty men exhausted scanty provisions during sixteen hours. Enjolras placed veto on fifteen hermetically sealed bottles found in cellar. Insurgents full of hope, smiled waiting for dawn attack, reckoned succor on way, divided day into three phases: six o'clock—regiment would turn; noon—insurrection of all Paris; sunset—revolution.

**Enjolras on insurrection and repression**: Insurrection speedily exhausted, has only certain number of shots and combatants. Empty cartridge-box and dead man cannot be replaced. Repression has army, does not count men; has Vincennes, does not count shots. Struggles of one against hundred always crush barricade unless revolution flings flaming archangel's sword into balance. Then everything rises, pavements seethe, popular redoubts abound, Paris quivers supremely, *quid divinum* given forth, a 10th of August or 29th of July in air, wonderful light appears, yawning maw of force draws back, army sees before it erect and tranquil that prophet, France.

**Broader insurrection (6th June morning)**: Barricades begun in Rue du Poirier and Rue des Gravilliers. Young man armed with rifle attacked squadron of cavalry on open boulevard, killed commander, remarked "There's another who will do us no more harm," was put to sword. Woman fired on National Guard from behind lowered blind in Rue Saint-Denis. Child aged fourteen arrested in Rue de la Cossonerie with pockets full of cartridges. Entrance to Rue Bertin-Poirée received lively fusillade welcoming regiment of cuirassiers led by Marshal General Cavaignac de Barague. In Rue Planche-Mibray, old pottery and household utensils thrown on soldiers from roofs—bad sign. Marshal Soult grew thoughtful, recalled Suchet's saying at Saragossa: "We are lost when the old women empty their pots de chambre on our heads." Military chiefs made haste to stamp out these beginnings of conflagration. Delayed attack on barricades Maubuée, de la Chanvrerie and Saint-Merry until sparks extinguished, to deal with barricades only and finish at one blow. Columns thrown into streets where fermentation occurred, sweeping large, sounding small, right and left, now slowly and cautiously, now at full charge. Troops broke in doors of houses whence shots fired; cavalry dispersed groups on boulevards.

**Assailants' fire (6th June, ongoing)**: Musketry and grape-shot alternated without great ravages. Top of Corinthe façade suffered; window on first floor and attic window riddled with buckshot, slowly losing shape. Combatants posted there obliged to withdraw. Tactics: fire long to exhaust insurgents' ammunition; when firing slackens, assault made. Mattress incident: old woman placed mattress in front of attic window on roof of six-story house slightly beyond barricade, supported at bottom on two poles, upheld at top by two ropes attached to nails in window frames. Mattress fell outside barricade between besiegers and besieged. First cannon attack: eight-pounder brass cannon crew attacked; whole barricade fired but missed. Flame leaped from insurgent rifle, artillery-man turned twice with arms extended, head uplifted, fell with side on gun, ball traversed breast side to side. Dead. After sergeant's death, exasperated troop lying flat on stomachs opened fire on barricade.

**Further cannon operations (6th June, later)**: Two cannons attacked redoubt from Rue de la Chanvrerie; two others from Rue Saint-Denis and Rue Aubry-le-Boucher riddled Saint-Merry barricade. Four cannons echoed each other mournfully. Combatants driven from crest by balls and from cabaret windows by grape-shot. Attacking columns ventured into street without being picked off, attempted to scale redoubt briskly and suddenly. Barricade long silent, then poured forth desperate fire; seven or eight discharges followed with rage and joy. Street filled with blinding smoke. After minutes, two thirds of gunners distinguished lying beneath wheels of cannons. Those standing continued to serve pieces with severe tranquility but fire slackened. Smoke like fog filled street, rendered denser and thicker by lofty houses, rose gradually, incessantly renewed, creating twilight even in broad daylight. Combatants could hardly see each other from one end of street to other.

**Bossuet on Enjolras**: Admires Enjolras's impassive temerity. Lives alone, renders him sad; complains his greatness binds him to widowhood. Rest have mistresses who make them crazy, that is, brave. When man as much in love as tiger, least he can do is fight like lion. Roland killed for Angélique; heroism comes from women. Man without woman is pistol without trigger; woman sets man off. Enjolras has no woman, not in love, yet intrepid—thing unheard of that man should be cold as ice and bold as fire.

## Philosophical Context
Combeferre quoted and discussed classical figures—Harmodius and Aristogiton, Brutus, Chereas, Stephanus, Cromwell, Charlotte Corday, Sand. Discussion reverted to Brutus and Cæsar. Combeferre argued Cæsar fell justly; his twenty-three wounds touch less than spitting in face of Jesus Christ. Cæsar stabbed by senators; Christ cuffed by lackeys. One feels God through greater outrage. **Combeferre on war and kings**: When no more kings, there will be no more war. Remarked sergeant was charming young man, intrepid, thoughtful, well-educated, probably in love, not more than five and twenty, might be someone's brother.
